extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (esp. empiricism/Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize John Locke's substantive claims about the origin, classification, and limits of ideas (simple vs. complex), including how sensation and reflection furnish the understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinking consists in consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking properly consists in being conscious that one thinks; to say the soul always thinks but the man is not always conscious of it is unintelligible and creates a problematic duality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues against the notion that the soul can think without the person's consciousness; analogy: saying a body is extended without parts is as unintelligible as saying thinking occurs without self-perception. He uses examples (sleeping people, infants) to show that absence of conscious thought is common and cannot be overridden by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ideas but from Sensation and Reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: All ideas in the understanding originate only from two sources: sensation (impressions from external objects through the senses) and reflection (the mind’s observation of its own operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke states this as a central empirical principle: the understanding is furnished by senses and reflection and then can compound, compare, and abstract, but not invent simple ideas beyond those inputs. He cites observation of children as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant and fetal states show lack of innate ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: New-born infants and fetuses show few signs of thinking or reasoning; much of their time is sleep and perception is limited to urgent bodily needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as empirical support against innate or pre-existing ideas: because newborns lack the material of ideas (limited sense input), they lack complex thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind thinks in proportion to experiential matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercise and extent of thinking increase as the mind receives more material (ideas) from experience; as sensory input grows, faculties like remembering, imagining, and reasoning develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of child development: familiarity with persons/objects produces distinguishable retained ideas; the mind advances by compounding and reflecting on ideas obtained from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas begin with first sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: A person begins to have ideas when he first experiences sensation, which is an impression or motion made in some part of the body that the understanding notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines sensation as the initial inlet of ideas into the mind and ties the origin of ideas to bodily impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impressions and reflection are the original of all knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge originates from (1) impressions made by outward objects on the senses and (2) the mind’s own operations reflected upon; all higher thoughts are built from these materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke frames these two processes as the groundwork from which all ideas, even sublime speculations, ultimately derive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding passive in reception of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: In receiving simple ideas the understanding is for the most part passive; it cannot refuse to have or alter those ideas once impressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the mind is like a mirror that cannot prevent images impressed upon it; objects of the senses often ‘obtrude’ ideas whether we will or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: simple ideas vs complex ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ideas are simple (uncompounded, uniform appearances) and some complex (compounded from simples); simple ideas are the basic materials of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes that simple ideas are distinct even when multiple senses are engaged simultaneously (e.g., cold and hardness are distinct ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind cannot invent or destroy simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: No amount of intellectual effort can create a new simple idea not derived from sensation or reflection, nor can the understanding destroy simple ideas once imprinted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke invites thought-experiments (try to imagine a taste never experienced) and analogous cases (blind persons cannot have color ideas) to show limits of imagination relative to sensory experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only qualities that affect the senses are imaginable
rubrics_metrics.description: Human imagination is limited to qualities that can affect our senses (sounds, tastes, smells, visible and tangible qualities); qualities of hypothetical extra senses are beyond our conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke allows that other creatures might have other senses, but for humans it’s presumptuous to imagine qualities beyond sensory capacities; he follows common opinion of five senses while acknowledging possible additional ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of simple ideas of sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas of sensation can be divided into: (1) those received by one sense only, (2) those conveyed by more than one sense, (3) those from reflection only, and (4) those suggested by both sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a taxonomy to organize how various ideas enter the mind; examples include colors (one sense) vs extension/motion (multiple senses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Many simple sensory ideas lack specific names
rubrics_metrics.description: There are far more distinct sensory ideas (e.g., smells, tastes) than we have words for; language supplies only general epithets for many varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that sweet/stinking suffice for many smells though the sensations are distinct; his enumeration will list only ideas material to his purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of solidity arises from touch
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of solidity (impenetrability/resistance) is derived from touch: solidity is that which hinders the approach of two bodies and is essential to the concept of body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke defines solidity, distinguishes it from space and hardness, and uses physical examples (water in a golden globe in a press) to explain solidity’s properties and its role in impulse, resistance, and protrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidity fills space and is distinct from space
rubrics_metrics.description: Solidity is the filling of space that excludes other bodies (resistance), and must be distinguished from pure space (which has neither resistance nor motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He explains we can form an idea of empty space apart from solidity; solidity is an idea of something that resists or protrudes into space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidity differs from hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Solidity (impenetrability) is different from hardness (cohesion and resistance to change of figure); even soft bodies can be as solid as hard ones in the sense of excluding other bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses thought/physical experiments (air in a football, water in a sealed globe) to show that softness does not negate solidity understood as resistance to displacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas received by both sight and touch: space-related ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ideas—space/extension, figure, rest, and motion—are perceivable both by sight and touch and belong to that class of multi-sensory simple ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke enumerates these as important ideas and defers further detailed treatment elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas of reflection: perception and volition
rubrics_metrics.description: When the mind reflects on its own operations it acquires simple ideas such as perception/thinking and volition/willing; these correspond to faculties called understanding and will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes modes of these reflective ideas (remembrance, discerning, reasoning, judging, knowledge, faith) will be discussed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas suggested by both sensation and reflection: pleasure, pain, power, existence, unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain basic ideas (pleasure/delight and pain/uneasiness, power, existence, unity, and succession) are suggested by both external sensation and internal reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains pleasure and pain are nearly universal accompaniments of ideas and serve as motives for action; he discusses the uses of pain (warning, preservation) and broader theological ends (leading to seeking completeness in God).

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession as idea from reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of succession (train of ideas passing one after another) is suggested more by inner mental experience than outward senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke points to the continual passing of ideas in consciousness as the source of this simple idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are the materials of all knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple ideas enumerated (and others) form the raw materials from which all complex ideas and the whole of human knowledge are constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke invites readers to appreciate how few simple ideas can combine into vast varieties of complex thoughts (analogy of letters making many words; extension offering infinite mathematical possibilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privative causes still produce positive ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Some simple ideas in the mind arise from privations (e.g., darkness) yet are as positive and distinct in the understanding as ideas caused by positive qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the mental idea from the external physical cause; a person can have clear ideas of black or white without knowing the physical mechanisms that produce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas in mind are distinct from their external causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas we have (e.g., of colour, motion) are to be treated as mental items distinct from inquiries into the physical causes that produce corresponding sensations in external things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes methodological separation: perceiving/knowing the idea is different from investigating how external particles produce that perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: One may possess ideas without knowing their physical causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner (painter or dyer) can have clearer ideas of colours than a philosopher who analyzes their causes; knowledge of causes is not necessary for clear mental ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show the independence of clear mental conception from scientific or causal explanation.
